### Purpose
Production HTTP gateways mediate diverse client-upstream interactions, requiring distinct connection, first-byte (TTFB), idle-stream, and total-request timeouts. A single overarching timeout cannot safely govern these interactions; setting it high permits slow-loris denial-of-service, while setting it low breaks legitimate long-lived transfers. Layering these timers decouples transport-level health from application latency, preserving partial streaming responses—such as large payloads or server-sent events—while defending network resources against anomalous stalls at every transaction phase.

### Failure modes
Each timeout addresses unique failure domains. A connection timeout mitigates TCP handshake drops, SYN floods, or unreachable hosts. A first-byte timeout bounds upstream application processing, catching database deadlocks or thread starvation before any data transfers. Without an idle-stream timeout, stalled read/write operations during chunked transfers hang indefinitely, trapping gateway buffers. Crucially, a total-request timeout serves as the ultimate safety boundary, terminating pathological slow transfers that trick idle timers by sending sporadic single-byte keep-alives.

### Operational guidance
Enforcing this separation guarantees deterministic connection-pool cleanup and prevents socket exhaustion by reclaiming inactive file descriptors. When any boundary expires, the gateway must trigger proactive cancellation propagation, sending RST packets downstream and issuing HTTP/2 `RST_STREAM` frames or closing TCP sockets upstream. This actively halts backend processing rather than leaving orphaned tasks consuming compute. For operational tuning, set strict connection limits (1–3 seconds), bounded first-byte thresholds pegged to p99 service-level objectives, moderate idle-stream windows (15–30 seconds) to tolerate transient network jitter, and absolute total-request caps based on business limits.

Tune the connection, first-byte, and idle-stream timeouts tightly to detect discrete stalls early, reserving the total-request timeout strictly as a non-negotiable absolute backstop.
